morocco/jemaa-el-fnaa.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
morocco/jemaa-el-fnaa.description: Marrakech's great main square, quiet by day and by evening filled with food stalls, storytellers, musicians and crowds.
morocco/jemaa-el-fnaa.details: Jemaa el-Fnaa is the heart of the Marrakech medina and is recognised by UNESCO for its tradition of oral storytelling and street performance. By day it is relatively quiet, with orange-juice sellers and a few entertainers, while from late afternoon rows of food stalls set up and the square fills with smoke, music and onlookers. Photographing performers usually leads to a request for payment, and touts are persistent. Rooftop cafes around the edge give a calm view over the whole scene.

morocco/marrakech-souks.name: Marrakech souks
morocco/marrakech-souks.description: A maze of covered lanes north of Jemaa el-Fnaa, with stalls grouped by trade selling leather, metalwork, spices and textiles.
morocco/marrakech-souks.details: The souks fan out north of the main square in narrow lanes that are traditionally organised by craft, with dyers, metalworkers, leather sellers and spice merchants each in their own area. Bargaining is the norm and a first quoted amount is rarely the final one. The layout is confusing and the lanes are shared with motorbikes, so it is easy to get lost, and a hired guide or a map app helps. Mornings are quieter and cooler than the afternoon.

morocco/koutoubia-mosque.name: Koutoubia Mosque
morocco/koutoubia-mosque.description: The twelfth-century minaret that dominates the Marrakech skyline, a model for later towers in Morocco and Spain.
morocco/koutoubia-mosque.details: The Koutoubia is the largest mosque in Marrakech, and its minaret, about seventy metres high, is built of sandstone with decorative panels that vary on each face. It served as the pattern for the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat. Only Muslims may enter the mosque itself, so non-Muslim visitors see the minaret from the gardens around it. It is at its best in the late afternoon light, and the gardens are free and open.

morocco/bahia-palace.name: Bahia Palace
morocco/bahia-palace.description: A nineteenth-century palace of tiled courtyards, painted cedar ceilings and gardens, built for a grand vizier.
morocco/bahia-palace.details: The Bahia Palace was built in the late nineteenth century for a powerful vizier and expanded by his son, in a style that mixes Moroccan and Andalusian traditions. Rooms open onto shaded courtyards of zellige tile, carved stucco and painted cedar ceilings, and a large garden courtyard sits at the centre. Parts of the building are closed to visitors, as it is still used for official purposes. Midday groups can be noisy, so arriving early makes it feel calmer.

morocco/saadian-tombs.name: Saadian Tombs
morocco/saadian-tombs.description: A royal burial ground of the sixteenth century, sealed off for centuries and rediscovered in the early twentieth.
morocco/saadian-tombs.details: The Saadian Tombs hold members of the dynasty that ruled Morocco in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, in mausoleums with lavish carved stucco and marble. A later ruler walled the complex off, and it was effectively forgotten until it was seen from the air in 1917. The Hall of Twelve Columns is the best-known chamber. The site is small and gets crowded quickly, so queueing is common at midday.

morocco/el-badi-palace.name: El Badi Palace
morocco/el-badi-palace.description: The ruins of a vast sixteenth-century palace, with sunken gardens, orange trees and storks nesting on the walls.
morocco/el-badi-palace.details: El Badi was built in the late sixteenth century by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, and its richest decoration was stripped by a later ruler to adorn his own capital. What survives is a large empty courtyard with sunken gardens and pools, backed by high pisé walls where white storks nest. Underground passages and a small museum with a carved minbar can also be visited. The ruins are open and exposed, so sun protection helps.

morocco/majorelle-garden.name: Majorelle Garden
morocco/majorelle-garden.description: A cactus and bamboo garden with strikingly cobalt-blue buildings, created by a French painter and later restored by Yves Saint Laurent.
morocco/majorelle-garden.details: The garden was laid out from the 1920s by the French painter Jacques Majorelle, who painted its buildings in an intense cobalt blue that is now known by his name. It was bought and restored in 1980 by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé. Paths wind among cacti, bamboo and water features, and a small museum on Amazigh culture sits inside. It gets very crowded, and timed tickets purchased ahead avoid a long queue.

morocco/ben-youssef-madrasa.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
morocco/ben-youssef-madrasa.description: A former Islamic college in the medina, with a central courtyard of carved cedar, stucco and tile and rows of tiny student cells.
morocco/ben-youssef-madrasa.details: The Ben Youssef was a school for Quranic study, rebuilt in the sixteenth century into one of the largest madrasas in Morocco. A central courtyard with a pool is lined with carved cedar, plasterwork and zellige tile, and around it rise two storeys of small cells that once housed students. It reopened after a lengthy restoration and is a good place to see traditional decorative arts up close. Light is best in the morning, and the narrow stairs can be crowded.

morocco/marrakech-hammam.name: Traditional hammam
morocco/marrakech-hammam.description: A steam bath followed by a scrub, a long-standing part of Moroccan daily life, offered at a local bathhouse or a spa.
morocco/marrakech-hammam.details: A hammam is a public steam bath where bathers move through rooms of increasing heat, are scrubbed with a rough mitt and black soap, and rinse with buckets of water. Local hammams are communal and simple, while spas in the medina offer a gentler, private version with a massage. Swimwear or disposable underwear is normally worn, and separate hours or sections apply for men and women. It is a good way to relax tired legs.

morocco/marrakech-cooking-class.name: Moroccan cooking class
morocco/marrakech-cooking-class.description: A hands-on class, often starting with a market visit, in which you learn to make tagine, couscous and salads.
morocco/marrakech-cooking-class.details: Cooking classes in Marrakech usually begin with a short trip through the market to choose vegetables, spices and meat, then move to a riad kitchen or a garden setting. Typical dishes include a tagine, a selection of cooked salads and a sweet pastry or tea. Groups are small and vegetarian options are generally available if requested ahead. You eat the meal you have prepared at the end.

morocco/imlil-village-walk.name: Imlil village walk
morocco/imlil-village-walk.description: A gentle walk around a High Atlas village at the foot of Mount Toubkal, on mule tracks between terraces and walnut trees.
morocco/imlil-village-walk.details: Imlil sits in a valley at the base of the Toubkal massif, around an hour and a half from Marrakech, and is the trailhead for the climb to North Africa's highest peak. Short walks lead from the village to neighbouring settlements across terraced fields and past walnut groves. It is noticeably cooler than Marrakech, and the air is much clearer. Paths are rocky and can be slippery after rain or snow.

morocco/imlil-atlas-hike.name: High Atlas village hike
morocco/imlil-atlas-hike.description: A guided walk of several hours between Berber villages near Imlil, with views toward Mount Toubkal.
morocco/imlil-atlas-hike.details: A guided hike from Imlil follows mule paths between villages such as Aremd and Tamatert, climbing through terraced fields and juniper slopes with views of the Toubkal massif. The routes are suitable for reasonably fit walkers without climbing experience. Weather in the mountains can turn quickly, and winter snow can close higher paths. Tea in a village house or on a terrace is usually part of the day.

morocco/essaouira-medina.name: Essaouira medina and ramparts
morocco/essaouira-medina.description: A whitewashed, wind-swept Atlantic port town with an eighteenth-century fortified medina and cannons along its sea wall.
morocco/essaouira-medina.details: Essaouira's walled medina was laid out in the eighteenth century and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with white and blue buildings and a layout that is easier to follow than in many Moroccan cities. The Skala de la Ville, a sea wall lined with old cannons, gives views over the Atlantic and the island fortress offshore. Craftsmen working thuya wood sell their goods in small workshops. It is windy for much of the year, so a jacket is useful even in summer.

morocco/essaouira-port.name: Essaouira fishing port
morocco/essaouira-port.description: A busy harbour of blue wooden boats, with fish stalls where the day's catch is grilled to order.
morocco/essaouira-port.details: The port at Essaouira is a working harbour where boats unload the catch each afternoon, and rows of stalls sell fresh fish and shellfish that are grilled on the spot. Visitors choose fish from the display, agree the price and sit at communal tables. The harbour is noisy and busy, with seagulls constantly overhead. Care is needed on the slippery quayside.

image.title: File:Fishing boats in the port of Essaouira, 2008.jpg
image.author: DimiTalen

morocco/essaouira-beach.name: Essaouira beach
morocco/essaouira-beach.description: A long, windy Atlantic beach popular with kitesurfers and windsurfers, with camels and horses for hire along the sand.
morocco/essaouira-beach.details: The beach stretches south of the town and is famous for its steady winds, which draw kitesurfers and windsurfers for much of the year. The wind makes it better for activity than lounging, and the water is cool. Schools offer lessons and equipment hire. Camel and horse rides are available at the southern end.

morocco/ait-benhaddou.name: Ait Benhaddou
morocco/ait-benhaddou.description: A fortified earthen village on the old caravan route to the Sahara, a UNESCO site used as a film location.
morocco/ait-benhaddou.details: Ait Benhaddou is a ksar, a cluster of fortified clay houses climbing a hillside above a river, and it once served as a stop on the caravan route between the Sahara and Marrakech. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has appeared in many films and television series. A handful of families still live inside, but most residents now live in the newer village across the river. The walk up through the ksar involves steps and uneven ground and gives a view over the valley.

morocco/skoura-palm-grove.name: Skoura palm grove and kasbah
morocco/skoura-palm-grove.description: A green oasis of date palms and old mud-brick kasbahs near Ouarzazate, quiet compared with the main tourist route.
morocco/skoura-palm-grove.details: Skoura is a palm grove on the edge of the desert, scattered with fortified kasbahs of earthen brick, some of them converted into guesthouses. Walking or cycling through the grove on shaded tracks gives a look at the irrigation channels and small farms that depend on them. It is much quieter than Ait Benhaddou or Ouarzazate. Some kasbahs can be visited for a small fee.

morocco/todra-gorge.name: Todra Gorge
morocco/todra-gorge.description: A narrow canyon of sheer limestone walls up to about 300 metres high, with a stream and palm groves at the base.
morocco/todra-gorge.details: The Todra Gorge cuts through the High Atlas near Tinghir, and at its narrowest the walls rise almost straight up on both sides with only a stream and a road between them. A palm grove fills the valley below the gorge. Walking up the gorge is easy and flat, and climbers use the cliffs. It is at its best in the morning light and gets crowded when tour groups arrive at midday.

morocco/dades-gorge.name: Dades Gorge
morocco/dades-gorge.description: A winding valley of red rock formations and kasbahs, known for rock towers nicknamed the monkey fingers and a switchback road.
morocco/dades-gorge.details: The Dades valley runs north from Boumalne Dades between kasbahs and green fields, with eroded rock towers that locals call monkey fingers and a road that doubles back in tight hairpin bends. The scenery is best in the early morning and late afternoon light. A good view of the road can be had from a roadside cafe at the top of the hairpins. Roads in the upper gorge can be rough, and winter conditions are cold.

morocco/erg-chebbi-camel-trek.name: Camel trek in the Erg Chebbi dunes
morocco/erg-chebbi-camel-trek.description: A late-afternoon camel ride into the Sahara's tallest dunes in Morocco, ending at a camp for the night.
morocco/erg-chebbi-camel-trek.details: Erg Chebbi is a sea of orange sand dunes, some rising over a hundred metres, at the edge of the Sahara near Merzouga. Camels carry visitors into the dunes in the afternoon for sunset, and most then stay at a desert camp with dinner, music around a fire and a very dark sky. Sunrise is the other great moment, and it is cold at night. Camp facilities are basic, and sandstorms can interrupt the plan.

morocco/merzouga-4x4-dunes.name: Dune 4x4 and sandboarding in Merzouga
morocco/merzouga-4x4-dunes.description: A morning in 4x4 vehicles across the desert around Merzouga, with a stop to slide down the dunes on a board.
morocco/merzouga-4x4-dunes.details: Local guides drive 4x4s across the flat desert and up to the dunes, stopping at an oasis and sometimes a nomad family's tent. Sandboarding on the dune face is available at most operators and is easier than it looks, but climbing back up is tiring. Early morning is cooler and quieter. Sand gets everywhere, so protect cameras and phones.

morocco/fes-medina.name: Fes el-Bali medina walk
morocco/fes-medina.description: The old walled city of Fes, a UNESCO site of thousands of lanes and one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world.
morocco/fes-medina.details: Fes el-Bali was founded around the turn of the ninth century and remains a living city, with workshops, mosques, fountains and homes packed into a maze of narrow lanes that mules still use to haul goods. The al-Qarawiyyin mosque and university, founded in 859, sit at its core, though non-Muslims cannot enter. It is very easy to get lost, and a licensed guide for the first day makes a large difference. The lanes are steep, uneven and busy, and mules have right of way.

image.title: File:Terrasses de Fès el Bali - A858.jpg
image.author: Passet Stéphane

morocco/chouara-tannery.name: Chouara Tannery
morocco/chouara-tannery.description: The oldest leather tannery in Fes, a honeycomb of stone dye vats viewed from the terraces of surrounding leather shops.
morocco/chouara-tannery.details: Leather has been tanned at Chouara by hand since the medieval period, in rows of stone vats of dye and pigeon-dropping solution used to soften hides. Visitors look down on the work from the upper terraces of the leather shops around it, and staff hand out sprigs of mint to hold against the smell. There is no entry charge but the shops expect that you will look around their goods. The work is hard to watch for some people, and the smell is strong in warm weather.

morocco/bou-inania-madrasa.name: Bou Inania Madrasa
morocco/bou-inania-madrasa.description: A fourteenth-century religious college in Fes with a tiled courtyard and carved cedar, open to non-Muslim visitors.
morocco/bou-inania-madrasa.details: The Bou Inania was built in the fourteenth century under the Marinid dynasty and is one of few religious buildings in Fes that non-Muslims may enter. Its central courtyard has a fountain, walls covered in zellige tile and carved stucco, and finely carved cedar screens. It is still a working religious site, so visitors are asked to dress and behave respectfully. It is compact and quick to see.

morocco/fes-el-jdid.name: Fes el-Jdid and the Mellah
morocco/fes-el-jdid.description: The thirteenth-century royal quarter of Fes, with the brass doors of the Royal Palace and the old Jewish quarter behind it.
morocco/fes-el-jdid.details: Fes el-Jdid, or New Fes, was built by the Marinid dynasty in the thirteenth century as a royal and administrative district beside the older medina. The gilded entrance doors of the Royal Palace are the usual stop, though the palace itself is closed to the public. Behind it lies the Mellah, the former Jewish quarter, with distinctive wooden balconies that differ from the rest of the city. A Jewish cemetery and a restored synagogue can be visited. The district is much quieter than the medina.

morocco/merenid-tombs.name: Merenid Tombs viewpoint
morocco/merenid-tombs.description: The ruins of fourteenth-century royal tombs on a hill above Fes, with the best view over the whole old city.
morocco/merenid-tombs.details: The Merenid Tombs are ruined tombs of Marinid rulers on a ridge north of the medina, and the real reason to come is the view from them, which spreads out over the rooftops, minarets and tanneries of Fes el-Bali. It is the classic place to see the city at sunset. There is a short, steep walk up from the road, or a taxi to the top. It is exposed and breezy in the evening.

morocco/volubilis.name: Volubilis and Moulay Idriss
morocco/volubilis.description: The best-preserved Roman ruins in Morocco, with mosaic floors still in place, near a hilltop pilgrimage town.
morocco/volubilis.details: Volubilis was the main Roman city in the province of Mauretania Tingitana and was later occupied by Idris I, founder of the first Moroccan dynasty. Its ruins, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, include a triumphal arch, a basilica and a number of villas with mosaic floors still on site. The setting among olive groves and cornfields is striking, and shade is limited. Nearby, the hilltop town of Moulay Idriss is a sacred pilgrimage site that is a popular add-on.

image.title: File:The Roman Ruins of Volubilis - Morocco.jpg
image.author: Mustang Joe

morocco/chefchaouen-blue-medina.name: Chefchaouen blue medina
morocco/chefchaouen-blue-medina.description: A small mountain town in the Rif whose medina is washed in shades of blue, with steep alleys and a central square.
morocco/chefchaouen-blue-medina.details: Chefchaouen was founded in the late fifteenth century as a fortress and later became home to Muslim and Jewish refugees from Spain. Its medina is painted in shades of blue and white, the origin of which is debated, and is small enough to explore on foot. Alleys climb through steps and arches to hilltop views. It is cooler than the plains, and early morning is the best time for photography.

morocco/spanish-mosque-viewpoint.name: Spanish Mosque viewpoint
morocco/spanish-mosque-viewpoint.description: A hilltop ruin above Chefchaouen reached by a short walk, giving a view over the blue town at sunset.
morocco/spanish-mosque-viewpoint.details: The Spanish Mosque is a disused building on a hill east of Chefchaouen that is not really visited for its architecture but for the view down over the town, backed by the Rif mountains. The path is a steady walk of around half an hour from the edge of the medina. Sunset is the popular time, so it gets busy at the viewing point. The path is rocky and unlit, so allow time to get down before dark.

morocco/akchour-waterfalls.name: Akchour waterfalls hike
morocco/akchour-waterfalls.description: A walk up a river valley in the Rif to waterfalls and swimming pools, with a natural stone arch further on.
morocco/akchour-waterfalls.details: Akchour, about an hour from Chefchaouen, is a village at the start of trails along a river through a wooded valley to a series of waterfalls and pools. The walk to the nearest falls is moderate and popular, and a longer route continues to a natural rock arch known as God's Bridge. Paths are rocky and cross the stream, so good footwear helps. Swimming is possible in the pools in warm months.

morocco/hassan-ii-mosque.name: Hassan II Mosque
morocco/hassan-ii-mosque.description: A vast mosque built partly over the Atlantic in Casablanca, with one of the tallest minarets in the world.
morocco/hassan-ii-mosque.details: The Hassan II Mosque was completed in 1993 and stands on a platform extending over the ocean, with a minaret roughly two hundred metres high. The prayer hall holds tens of thousands of worshippers, and has a sliding roof and a glass floor panel. It is one of the few mosques in Morocco that non-Muslims can enter, but only by guided tour at set times, so check the schedule. Its scale is the main impression, and the sea wind on the platform is strong.

morocco/habous-quarter.name: Habous Quarter
morocco/habous-quarter.description: Casablanca's 1930s new medina, laid out by French planners in Moroccan style with arcades, craft shops and pastry stalls.
morocco/habous-quarter.details: The Habous quarter, also called the new medina, was built in the 1930s under the French protectorate to rehouse residents in a traditional style, with arcaded streets, a mosque and a royal palace. Today it is known for its bookshops, craft shops and pastry makers, and is quieter and cleaner than the old medinas elsewhere. It is flat and easy to walk. Most shops close in the middle of the day on Fridays.

morocco/kasbah-of-the-udayas.name: Kasbah of the Udayas
morocco/kasbah-of-the-udayas.description: A twelfth-century fortress above the Rabat estuary, with blue-and-white lanes and a quiet Andalusian garden.
morocco/kasbah-of-the-udayas.details: The Kasbah of the Udayas is a walled fortress at the mouth of the Bou Regreg river, begun by the Almohad dynasty in the twelfth century. Inside, narrow lanes of blue-and-white houses lead to a viewing terrace over the river and Atlantic. An Andalusian garden and a cafe serving mint tea sit within the walls. The kasbah is small and calm and quick to explore.

image.title: File:Ruelle bleue, Kasbah des Oudayas (Rabat, Maroc) (15561666480).jpg
image.author: Carlos ZGZ from Paris, France

morocco/hassan-tower.name: Hassan Tower and the Mausoleum of Mohammed V
morocco/hassan-tower.description: The unfinished minaret of a twelfth-century mosque in Rabat, beside a royal mausoleum guarded by ceremonial horsemen.
morocco/hassan-tower.details: The Hassan Tower was begun in the late twelfth century as the minaret of what would have been one of the largest mosques in the world, but work stopped when the sultan died, leaving rows of columns and an unfinished tower. Across the esplanade stands the white-marble Mausoleum of Mohammed V, built in the 1960s, where ceremonial guards stand at the entrance. Non-Muslim visitors can enter the mausoleum. The esplanade is open and exposed.

morocco/chellah.name: Chellah necropolis
morocco/chellah.description: A walled complex of Roman and medieval ruins on the edge of Rabat, with storks nesting on its minaret and gardens.
morocco/chellah.details: Chellah sits on the site of the Roman town of Sala Colonia and later became a burial ground of the Marinid dynasty. Inside the walls are Roman streets and monuments next to a ruined mosque and tombs, in an overgrown garden. White storks nest on the old minaret and walls. The paths are uneven and the site is quiet outside peak hours.

morocco.name: Morocco
morocco.description: A North African country of walled medinas, High Atlas valleys and Saharan dunes, within easy reach of Europe.

morocco/marrakech-safi.name: Marrakech-Safi
morocco/marrakech-safi.description: The region around Marrakech, taking in the High Atlas foothills and the Atlantic port of Essaouira.

morocco/marrakech.name: Marrakech
morocco/marrakech.description: A red-walled city of souks, palaces and a vast main square, the usual starting point for trips into the Atlas and Sahara.

morocco/imlil.name: Imlil
morocco/imlil.description: A High Atlas village at the foot of Mount Toubkal, used for walks between Berber villages and as the trailhead for the climb.

morocco/essaouira.name: Essaouira
morocco/essaouira.description: A whitewashed Atlantic port with a fortified medina, a busy fishing harbour and steady winds for kitesurfing.

morocco/draa-tafilalet.name: Draa-Tafilalet
morocco/draa-tafilalet.description: The south-eastern region that stretches from the High Atlas across the kasbah country to the edge of the Sahara.

morocco/ait-benhaddou.name: Ait Benhaddou
morocco/ait-benhaddou.description: A fortified earthen village on the old Saharan caravan route, listed by UNESCO and used as a film location.

morocco/skoura.name: Skoura
morocco/skoura.description: A palm grove oasis near Ouarzazate scattered with mud-brick kasbahs and far fewer visitors than the main route.

morocco/dades-valley.name: Dades Valley
morocco/dades-valley.description: A valley of red rock formations, kasbahs and a hairpin road on the route between Ouarzazate and the desert.

morocco/todra-gorge.name: Todra Gorge
morocco/todra-gorge.description: A narrow canyon with limestone walls some 300 metres high, near Tinghir on the route to the desert.

morocco/merzouga.name: Merzouga
morocco/merzouga.description: The village at the edge of the Erg Chebbi dunes, where camel treks and desert camps for the night begin.

morocco/fes-meknes.name: Fes-Meknes
morocco/fes-meknes.description: The northern region that holds the imperial cities of Fes and Meknes and the Roman ruins of Volubilis.

morocco/fes.name: Fes
morocco/fes.description: Morocco's oldest imperial city, with a vast car-free medieval medina, historic madrasas and working tanneries.

morocco/volubilis.name: Volubilis
morocco/volubilis.description: The best-preserved Roman site in Morocco, with mosaic floors in place, near the pilgrimage town of Moulay Idriss.

images.title: File:The Roman Ruins of Volubilis - Morocco.jpg
images.author: Mustang Joe

morocco/tanger-tetouan-al-hoceima.name: Tanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima
morocco/tanger-tetouan-al-hoceima.description: The northern region on the Mediterranean and Rif mountains, home to Tangier, Tetouan and Chefchaouen.

morocco/chefchaouen.name: Chefchaouen
morocco/chefchaouen.description: A small mountain town in the Rif known for its blue-washed medina and hiking in the surrounding hills.

morocco/casablanca-settat.name: Casablanca-Settat
morocco/casablanca-settat.description: The Atlantic coast region that centres on Morocco's largest city and its economic hub.

morocco/casablanca.name: Casablanca
morocco/casablanca.description: Morocco's biggest city, a modern Atlantic port best known for the vast Hassan II Mosque.

morocco/rabat-sale-kenitra.name: Rabat-Sale-Kenitra
morocco/rabat-sale-kenitra.description: The coastal region around the national capital, taking in Rabat, its twin city Sale and the Atlantic plain.

morocco/rabat.name: Rabat
morocco/rabat.description: Morocco's calm, tree-lined capital, with a twelfth-century kasbah, an unfinished minaret and Roman ruins at Chellah.
